cards.title: Maximal rational rigidity despite a quadratic-field diagonal correction
cards.formal: For infinitely many positive integers r, is there a matrix A∈C_r(ℚ,√2) with R_ℚ(A,r)=r²? Equivalently, for every R≥1 there exist r≥R, a rational 2r×2r matrix M and a rational diagonal matrix D such that rank_{ℚ(√2)}(M+√2·I_{2r})≤r, A=M+D, and every rational matrix Z with fewer than r² nonzero entries satisfies rank_ℚ(A+Z)>r. Membership in C_r already ensures R_{ℚ(√2)}(A,r)≤2r. No effective construction or bound on rational entry sizes is part of the source question.
cards.why: Would show that adjoining one quadratic irrational can reduce the number of entries needed to lower matrix rank from quadratic to linear, exposing an extreme field dependence of rigidity.
cards.status_note: Read the full field-dependent definitions, class construction and exact Problem 10; checked the author-hosted paper and later targeted literature searches through 12 September 2026. No resolution of the r² target in C_r(ℚ,√2) was located. The dated source remains the basis for open status.

cards.definitions: ℚ is the rational field and ℚ(√2)={a+b√2:a,b∈ℚ}, with (√2)²=2. I_{2r} is the identity matrix. Rank over a field is the dimension of the span of a matrix’s columns over that field. For A∈ℚ^{2r×2r} and an extension field L⊇ℚ, define R_L(A,r)=min{|{(i,j):Zᵢⱼ≠0}|: Z∈L^{2r×2r}, rank_L(A+Z)≤r}. The cost counts changed entries, regardless of their magnitudes or bit encodings. Set D_r(ℚ,√2)={M∈ℚ^{2r×2r}:rank_{ℚ(√2)}(M+√2·I_{2r})≤r} and C_r(ℚ,√2)={M+D:M∈D_r(ℚ,√2), D∈ℚ^{2r×2r} diagonal}. All off-diagonal entries of D are zero. The rational rigidity R_ℚ is also called strict rigidity here, because rational matrices have field of definition ℚ. Changes in a larger field are measured separately. For every rational 2r×2r matrix the general upper bound R_ℚ(A,r)≤r² holds, so the target equality is maximal possible rigidity at target rank r. Infinite occurrence means unbounded r, not all sufficiently large r.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that the stated maximal-rigidity matrices exist for unbounded r, or refute the statement by proving that for all sufficiently large r every A∈C_r(ℚ,√2) has rational rigidity strictly below r². A superlinear lower bound smaller than r², a constant-factor field separation, or finitely many verified examples does not settle this exact maximality question.

context_blocks.title: The allowed replacement field can matter
context_blocks.text: The matrix itself is rational in both comparisons. Only the field from which changed entries may be chosen differs. An irrational correction can lower rank even when rational corrections with the same sparse pattern cannot.

context_blocks.title: The source class has a built-in sparse extension-field correction
context_blocks.text: For A=M+D in the stated class, changing diagonal entries by √2·I−D reaches rank at most r over ℚ(√2). Thus at most 2r changes suffice over that field, while the conjecture asks for the maximal r² changes over ℚ.

context_blocks.title: The current source lower bound is linear
context_blocks.text: Theorem 7 gives a matrix in C_r with rational rigidity at least 3r−2 for every r≥3. This proves a separation, but is far below the exact quadratic target.

context_blocks.title: This is stronger than the preceding conjecture
context_blocks.text: Conjecture 9 asks for a superlinear rational rigidity lower bound with only linearly many extension-field changes. Problem 10 asks for maximal rational rigidity inside the specified class. The two questions have different answer thresholds.

cards.context:
The matrix itself is rational in both comparisons. Only the field from which changed entries may be chosen differs. An irrational correction can lower rank even when rational corrections with the same sparse pattern cannot.

For A=M+D in the stated class, changing diagonal entries by √2·I−D reaches rank at most r over ℚ(√2). Thus at most 2r changes suffice over that field, while the conjecture asks for the maximal r² changes over ℚ.

Theorem 7 gives a matrix in C_r with rational rigidity at least 3r−2 for every r≥3. This proves a separation, but is far below the exact quadratic target.

Conjecture 9 asks for a superlinear rational rigidity lower bound with only linearly many extension-field changes. Problem 10 asks for maximal rational rigidity inside the specified class. The two questions have different answer thresholds.

methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. We aim for benchmarks of 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. All three use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The possible 1,000-problem expansion has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The targets are 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. Top 100, Top 500 and the possible Top 1000 use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
